purpose: Two independent prompt cohorts reserved for frozen-candidate confirmation; never use these outputs or timings to select a policy.

cohorts.prompt: A community garden shares one water tank among six plots. Volunteers record the tank level each morning, but rainfall and watering times vary. Design a simple weekly watering plan that avoids emptying the tank while keeping seedlings alive. Explain which observations should change the plan and how to handle a missing measurement. Distinguish a useful estimate from a guaranteed supply. Give a small example involving a dry week, and explain why simply dividing the tank equally every day might waste water or neglect a plot with newly planted seeds.

A museum is moving fragile objects from storage into an exhibition. Each object must be photographed, inspected, packed, transported, and checked on arrival. Only one photographer and two trained handlers are available, and some boxes require both handlers. Describe a practical workflow that avoids lost records and unnecessary waiting. Explain how to handle an object whose inspection finds damage, and how the team should recover if a transport trip is cancelled. Identify which steps can overlap and which must remain in order. Do not assume that every object takes the same time.

A program writes a configuration file that another process reads periodically. Sometimes the reader sees half of a newly written file and fails. Propose a robust update procedure using a temporary file and an atomic replacement. Explain what should happen when writing fails, when the application crashes before replacement, and when two writers attempt an update at once. Separate protection against partial files from protection against lost updates. Include a brief example of the sequence of operations and discuss what additional care is needed if durability after a power failure is required.

A school wants to compare two ways of teaching vocabulary. One class uses flash cards in the morning and another class plays a word game after lunch. Their teachers, ages, and attendance differ. Explain why the final quiz scores alone cannot establish which method works better. Propose a modest study that would make the comparison more useful without excluding pupils who need extra support. Discuss practice effects, missing quizzes, and the difference between remembering words tomorrow and remembering them next month. Give an example of a conclusion the study could support and one it could not.

A mobile application downloads a large map over an unreliable connection. Users can pause the download, restart the application, and switch between networks. Describe a design that resumes safely without treating a damaged partial file as a complete map. Explain how to identify which version is being downloaded, verify downloaded pieces, and publish the completed file. Discuss what to do when the remote map changes during the download. Compare the role of a checksum with the role of a version identifier, and explain why storing only the number of bytes already received is insufficient.

A small bakery prepares bread and pastries using one oven with two shelves. Some recipes require different temperatures, and opening the door delays baking. Customer orders arrive throughout the morning, with a few promised pickup times. Outline a scheduling approach that balances oven utilization with reliable pickup times. Explain why grouping every recipe of the same temperature together may be unfair to later orders. Describe how the baker should revise the plan after an urgent order or a failed batch. Use a short example and identify assumptions that would need real timing measurements.

An online form lets people reserve seats for a workshop. Two people can submit a request for the last seat at nearly the same moment. Explain how the server can prevent overbooking while still handling retries after a network timeout. Distinguish checking whether a seat is available from actually reserving it. Describe the role of a transaction and an idempotency identifier. Discuss what response a retry should receive when the original request succeeded but the reply was lost, and how expired temporary reservations should be released without cancelling a completed reservation.

A neighborhood group measures noise near a construction site using inexpensive sensors. Readings differ between devices and sometimes jump when a truck passes directly beside one sensor. Explain how to summarize the measurements without hiding brief loud events or treating every spike as a permanent change. Discuss calibration, sensor placement, missing data, and time of day. Suggest a transparent way to compare a week before and a week after a change in working hours. Describe which limitations should accompany the results and why a single average cannot answer every concern residents may have.

A volunteer kitchen receives donated vegetables with uncertain quantities and freshness. It must plan meals for forty people using a limited refrigerator and two cooking stations. Describe a practical planning process that reduces waste while keeping meals predictable. Explain which ingredients should be used first, how to handle a late donation, and what information volunteers should record at the end of the day. Discuss the tradeoff between preparing everything early and waiting for a more accurate attendance count. Give an example of a fallback meal and identify assumptions that should be checked rather than guessed.

A service processes payment notifications delivered by an external provider. Notifications may arrive twice, out of order, or after a long delay. Explain how to maintain a reliable local record without charging a customer twice or moving an order backward to an older state. Describe what identifiers should be stored and when processing should be acknowledged. Discuss how to recover if the service crashes after changing the database but before acknowledging a notification. Separate duplicate detection from ordering rules, and give a small example with three notifications arriving in an unexpected order.

A town tests a new bus timetable on one route during a rainy month. Passenger counts increase, but a nearby train service also experiences frequent cancellations. Explain what evidence is needed before attributing the increase to the timetable. Propose a comparison that uses existing observations while acknowledging their limits. Discuss differences between peak and off-peak travel, school holidays, and passengers transferring from trains. Describe how the town could report uncertainty honestly, and give an example of a useful operational decision that does not require claiming the timetable caused every additional journey.

A desktop editor periodically saves recovery copies while the user continues typing. Saving a large document can take several seconds, and the user may close the document or rename it during that time. Design a recovery system that keeps a consistent snapshot without blocking every keystroke. Explain how to associate a saved copy with the correct document version, how to avoid replacing a newer recovery copy with an older one, and how to clean up abandoned temporary files. Discuss what should happen after a crash when several incomplete or complete copies are present.

A science club is comparing two materials used to insulate a cup of warm water. Cups have slightly different shapes, room temperature changes during the afternoon, and the thermometer takes time to settle. Explain how to design a fair small experiment using equipment the club already has. Discuss starting temperatures, measurement order, repeated trials, and how to record unexpected events. Describe a simple graph that would help interpret cooling over time. Explain why one final temperature reading is weaker evidence than a consistent pattern across comparable trials, without claiming that more decimal places guarantee accuracy.

A warehouse robot receives instructions to collect items from several shelves before returning to a packing station. Some aisles are narrow, and another robot may temporarily block a route. Describe a planning strategy that avoids repeatedly abandoning useful progress whenever a delay occurs. Explain which information should trigger replanning and which small delays can be tolerated. Discuss how to prevent two robots from waiting forever for each other. Give an example involving a blocked aisle and a priority order, and distinguish a shortest route from a plan that reliably finishes on time.

A web dashboard combines information from three services that refresh at different rates. Users sometimes see a total that does not match the displayed component values because updates arrive separately. Explain several ways to present the data consistently. Compare taking a shared snapshot, displaying timestamps, and delaying an update until related values are ready. Discuss what happens when one service becomes unavailable or returns old information. Describe a sensible interface behavior that helps users understand freshness without suggesting that data from different moments describes one exact instant.

A local repair cooperative wants to keep a useful stock of spare parts but has little storage space. A few parts are used every week, while others are rarely needed but take a long time to obtain. Describe an initial stocking policy and how it should change as records accumulate. Explain why average monthly usage is not enough to decide every quantity. Discuss delivery delays, substitutes, shared parts, and the cost of an unfinished repair. Give a small example of two parts that deserve different policies even if their annual usage is similar.
